claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has a coarse lamellar microstructure after conventional casting.
The initial alloy contains no intentional microalloying addition.
Adding 0.5–1 wt% Ti during melting is the proposed intervention.
A controlled cooling rate will promote precipitate formation at eutectic boundaries.
Ti addition during synthesis will induce in-situ formation of nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates.
The Ti-rich precipitates will form at or near eutectic interfaces.
Formation of the Ti-rich precipitates will refine the lamellar microstructure.
Ti addition will produce finely dispersed secondary phases along eutectic interfaces during solidification.
The interfacial precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Precipitate-associated microstructural refinement will promote more uniform deformation.
More uniform deformation and strain accommodation will improve ductility.
The Ti-modified alloy will have roughly 20% greater yield strength than the Ti-free baseline processed under identical conditions.
The Ti-modified alloy will have about 10% greater elongation to failure than the Ti-free baseline processed under identical conditions.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvements are expected under conventional casting when processing parameters other than Ti addition are held constant.
Changes in alloy composition or processing conditions may alter precipitate morphology and the resulting strength–ductility response.
The optimal Ti concentration and cooling rate needed to obtain the desired precipitate size and distribution are unknown.
